Week 3 · Phase 1: Foundations

Optimization for Deep Learning

Why training deep networks is a hard non-convex problem and how the practical toolbox (SGD, momentum, Adam/AdamW, learning-rate schedules, careful initialization, clipping and normalization layers) makes it work.

72 min read4 interactive demos14 figures13 code blocks10 exercises
Learning objectives

By the end of this week you should be able to:

  • Describe what the loss surface of a neural network looks like (saddles, plateaus, flat and sharp minima) and what that implies for optimizers.
  • Explain the bias-variance structure of mini-batch gradients and use the linear scaling rule and the gradient noise scale to reason about batch size.
  • Derive and implement momentum, Nesterov momentum, AdaGrad, RMSProp, Adam (with bias correction) and AdamW (with decoupled weight decay) from scratch.
  • Choose and implement learning-rate schedules: step decay, cosine annealing, linear warmup, cyclical rates and the one-cycle policy.
  • Derive the Xavier/Glorot and He initialization variances, and diagnose vanishing and exploding gradients, including the use of gradient clipping.
  • Write the forward and backward pass of BatchNorm, explain train versus eval behavior, and compare BatchNorm, LayerNorm and GroupNorm.
  • Run a controlled experiment comparing optimizers, initializations and learning rates, and read the resulting loss curves.

Week 2 gave you the machinery to compute gradients with backpropagation. This week is about what you do with them. Training a neural network means minimizing a function of millions or billions of parameters that is non-convex, noisy (because you only ever see a small batch of data per step), badly conditioned and full of strange geometry. Classical optimization theory says very little that is comforting about this setting. And yet a handful of simple, well-tuned ingredients make training reliably succeed: mini-batch stochastic gradient descent, momentum or Adam-style adaptive scaling, a learning-rate schedule with warmup, an initialization that preserves signal scale, gradient clipping for the cases where it does not, and normalization layers that keep activations well behaved.

You will meet each ingredient in the same way: first the intuition, then the math, then a few lines of code, then the failure modes. By the end you will have a mental checklist for the single most common debugging situation in deep learning: "my loss is not going down, or it is going down too slowly, or it blew up."

The geometry of neural network loss surfaces

Let L(θ)\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})L(θ) be the training loss as a function of all parameters θ∈Rd\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\R^dθ∈Rd. For linear regression with squared error L\mathcal{L}L is a convex quadratic: one basin, one minimum, and gradient descent with a small enough step is guaranteed to find it. A neural network breaks this in two ways. First, the composition of weight matrices and nonlinearities makes L\mathcal{L}L non-convex. Second, the parameterization has enormous symmetries: permute the hidden units of a layer (together with the matching rows and columns of neighbouring matrices) and you get exactly the same function, so a minimum always comes with at least ∏ℓnℓ!\prod_\ell n_\ell!∏ℓ​nℓ​! copies. Non-convexity is therefore not an accident but a structural feature.

It is worth being precise about what "non-convex" implies and does not imply. It does not imply that gradient descent is hopeless. What matters is which kinds of critical points (∇L=0\nabla\mathcal{L}=\mathbf{0}∇L=0) exist and how much of the surface is easy to descend.

Critical points: minima, maxima and saddles

At a critical point the behavior is governed by the Hessian H=∇2L(θ)∈Rd×d\mathbf{H}=\nabla^2\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\in\R^{d\times d}H=∇2L(θ)∈Rd×d, which is symmetric and therefore has real eigenvalues λ1≥⋯≥λd\lambda_1\ge\dots\ge\lambda_dλ1​≥⋯≥λd​. Writing a small displacement δ\boldsymbol{\delta}δ in the eigenbasis, the second-order Taylor expansion at a critical point is

L(θ+δ)≈L(θ)+12∑i=1dλi ci2,\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}+\boldsymbol{\delta}) \approx \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) + \tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^d \lambda_i\, c_i^2,L(θ+δ)≈L(θ)+21​i=1∑d​λi​ci2​,

where cic_ici​ is the coordinate of δ\boldsymbol{\delta}δ along eigenvector iii. If every λi>0\lambda_i>0λi​>0 you are at a local minimum, if every λi<0\lambda_i<0λi​<0 at a local maximum, and if the signs are mixed at a saddle point: the loss goes up in some directions and down in others.

Now count. In one dimension a critical point is a minimum or a maximum. In ddd dimensions, if you imagine the signs of the eigenvalues as independent coin flips, the probability that all ddd are positive is 2−d2^{-d}2−d. For d=106d=10^6d=106 essentially every critical point is a saddle, and local minima with a high loss are exponentially rare compared with saddles. This heuristic (from random matrix theory and spin-glass models) was made influential for deep learning by Dauphin et al. (2014) and Choromanska et al. (2015): in high dimensions the obstacle to optimization is not bad local minima but saddle points and the flat regions around them, where the gradient is tiny and progress is slow. Empirically, on real networks, the local minima that gradient methods reach tend to have training loss close to the global minimum.

The coin-flip argument is a heuristic

Hessian eigenvalues are not independent, and real losses are not random Gaussian fields. The argument explains why you should expect saddles to outnumber minima; it does not prove that every network trains well. Poor conditioning, dead ReLUs, bad initialization and wrong learning rates produce plenty of failures that have nothing to do with local minima.

Why do saddles hurt gradient descent? Near the saddle the gradient is small, so the step −η∇L-\eta\nabla\mathcal{L}−η∇L is small. In the negative-curvature direction the escape is exponential, c(t)∼c(0) (1+η∣λmin⁡∣)tc(t)\sim c(0)\,(1+\eta|\lambda_{\min}|)^tc(t)∼c(0)(1+η∣λmin​∣)t, but it starts from whatever tiny component of the iterate lies along that direction. If you start almost exactly on the stable manifold, you can sit near the saddle for a very long time. The noise in stochastic gradients is a feature here: it perturbs the iterate off the stable manifold almost immediately. You can see this in the optimizer race below, where momentum and adaptive methods escape the saddle faster than plain gradient descent.

Plateaus, ravines and ill-conditioning

Even when there is a clean minimum, descent can be slow because of the shape of the basin. Consider the quadratic f(θ)=12θ⊤Hθf(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\tfrac12\boldsymbol{\theta}^\top\mathbf{H}\boldsymbol{\theta}f(θ)=21​θ⊤Hθ with Hessian eigenvalues between λmin⁡>0\lambda_{\min}>0λmin​>0 and λmax⁡\lambda_{\max}λmax​. Gradient descent θ←θ−ηHθ\boldsymbol{\theta}\leftarrow\boldsymbol{\theta}-\eta\mathbf{H}\boldsymbol{\theta}θ←θ−ηHθ multiplies the coordinate along eigenvector iii by (1−ηλi)(1-\eta\lambda_i)(1−ηλi​) every step. Two facts follow immediately.

  1. It converges only if ∣1−ηλi∣<1|1-\eta\lambda_i|<1∣1−ηλi​∣<1 for all iii, i.e. η<2/λmax⁡\eta<2/\lambda_{\max}η<2/λmax​. The steepest direction limits the learning rate.
  2. The slowest direction contracts by 1−ηλmin⁡1-\eta\lambda_{\min}1−ηλmin​. With the best possible step η⋆=2/(λmax⁡+λmin⁡)\eta^\star=2/(\lambda_{\max}+\lambda_{\min})η⋆=2/(λmax​+λmin​) the per-step contraction factor is ρ=λmax⁡−λmin⁡λmax⁡+λmin⁡=κ−1κ+1,κ=λmax⁡λmin⁡.\rho=\frac{\lambda_{\max}-\lambda_{\min}}{\lambda_{\max}+\lambda_{\min}}=\frac{\kappa-1}{\kappa+1},\qquad \kappa=\frac{\lambda_{\max}}{\lambda_{\min}}.ρ=λmax​+λmin​λmax​−λmin​​=κ+1κ−1​,κ=λmin​λmax​​.

The condition number κ\kappaκ is the ratio of the steepest to the shallowest curvature. If κ=1000\kappa=1000κ=1000 you need roughly κln⁡(1/ε)/2≈500ln⁡(1/ε)\kappa\ln(1/\varepsilon)/2\approx 500\ln(1/\varepsilon)κln(1/ε)/2≈500ln(1/ε) steps to shrink the error by a factor ε\varepsilonε. Neural network Hessians are famously ill-conditioned: a few outlier eigenvalues (often about as many as there are classes) are far larger than a huge bulk of near-zero ones. This is why plain gradient descent zigzags across steep ravine walls while crawling along the floor, and why the optimizers in the next sections exist.

Flat versus sharp minima

Different minima can have identical training loss and very different generalization. The idea, going back to Hochreiter and Schmidhuber (1997), is that a flat minimum (small Hessian eigenvalues, a wide basin) is better than a sharp one (large eigenvalues, narrow basin), because the test loss surface is a slightly shifted version of the training loss surface (see the dashed curve in the landscape figure): at a flat minimum the shift costs little, at a sharp one it costs a lot. A measurement often used is the loss increase under a small random perturbation, or the largest Hessian eigenvalue λmax⁡(H)\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf{H})λmax​(H).

Keskar et al. (2017) reported that large-batch training tends to find sharper minima than small-batch training, and that this correlates with a generalization gap. This fed a popular picture: gradient noise from small batches "bounces" the iterate out of sharp basins and into flat ones. The picture is useful but has two caveats you should remember.

  • Sharpness depends on parameterization. Dinh et al. (2017) showed that for ReLU networks you can rescale one layer by α\alphaα and the next by 1/α1/\alpha1/α without changing the function, which changes the Hessian arbitrarily. A raw λmax⁡\lambda_{\max}λmax​ is thus not by itself a reliable predictor of generalization; scale-invariant sharpness measures are needed.
  • The batch-size gap can often be closed by retuning the learning rate and schedule (Goyal et al., 2017; Shallue et al., 2019), so the story is not "large batch = bad".

There is also a link between learning rate and sharpness that is purely dynamical. GD with step η\etaη on a quadratic diverges once λmax⁡>2/η\lambda_{\max}>2/\etaλmax​>2/η, so with a large learning rate the iterates can only live in regions where the sharpness is below 2/η2/\eta2/η (observed by Cohen et al. 2021 under the name "edge of stability"). A large learning rate acts as an implicit constraint that steers training toward flatter regions.

What to carry forward

Deep learning loss surfaces are mostly saddles and long, curved, ill-conditioned valleys with many roughly equivalent minima. The practical goals are therefore (i) make progress along shallow directions without diverging along steep ones (momentum, adaptivity, normalization), (ii) avoid starting in a region where gradients vanish or explode (initialization), and (iii) end in a wide, low basin (learning-rate schedule, noise, regularization).

Gradient descent variants and batch size

The training objective is an average over NNN examples, L(θ)=1N∑i=1Nℓi(θ)\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N \ell_i(\boldsymbol{\theta})L(θ)=N1​∑i=1N​ℓi​(θ), where ℓi\ell_iℓi​ is the loss on example iii. The three classical variants differ only in how many examples they use to estimate ∇L\nabla\mathcal{L}∇L.

Variant Examples per step Gradient Per-step cost Noise
Batch (full-batch) GD all NNN exact ∇L\nabla\mathcal{L}∇L O(N)O(N)O(N) none
Stochastic GD (SGD, B=1B=1B=1) 1 ∇ℓi\nabla\ell_i∇ℓi​ O(1)O(1)O(1) very high
Mini-batch SGD BBB (e.g. 32 to 4096) 1B∑i∈B∇ℓi\frac1B\sum_{i\in\mathcal{B}}\nabla\ell_iB1​∑i∈B​∇ℓi​ O(B)O(B)O(B) moderate, ∝1/B\propto 1/B∝1/B

In modern usage "SGD" almost always means mini-batch SGD: sample a batch B\mathcal{B}B of size BBB without replacement (one pass through a shuffled dataset is an epoch), compute the average gradient, step.

θt+1=θt−η gt,gt=1B∑i∈Bt∇ℓi(θt).\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1}=\boldsymbol{\theta}_t-\eta\,\boldsymbol{g}_t,\qquad \boldsymbol{g}_t=\frac1B\sum_{i\in\mathcal{B}_t}\nabla\ell_i(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t).θt+1​=θt​−ηgt​,gt​=B1​i∈Bt​∑​∇ℓi​(θt​).

Mini-batches win for three reasons: hardware (a GPU computes 256 examples in barely more time than 8, so per-example cost falls), statistics (the gradient of a random subset is an unbiased estimate of the full gradient, so you get a good direction at a fraction of the price) and generalization (the noise is helpful, see above).

Mini-batch gradients as noisy estimates

Let G=∇L(θ)\boldsymbol{G}=\nabla\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})G=∇L(θ) be the true gradient and let Σ\boldsymbol{\Sigma}Σ be the covariance of the per-example gradients ∇ℓi\nabla\ell_i∇ℓi​ (over a random example). For a batch of BBB examples drawn independently,

E[gB]=G,Cov⁡[gB]=1BΣ.\E[\boldsymbol{g}_B]=\boldsymbol{G},\qquad \Cov[\boldsymbol{g}_B]=\frac{1}{B}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}.E[gB​]=G,Cov[gB​]=B1​Σ.

(When sampling without replacement from a finite dataset there is an extra factor (N−B)/(N−1)(N-B)/(N-1)(N−B)/(N−1), which makes the noise vanish when B=NB=NB=N.) The expected squared error E∥gB−G∥2=tr⁡(Σ)/B\E\norm{\boldsymbol{g}_B-\boldsymbol{G}}^2=\tr(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})/BE∥gB​−G∥2=tr(Σ)/B falls like 1/B1/B1/B. The chart below shows this for a small network: the measured error follows the 1/B1/B1/B line and is much larger than the gradient itself for tiny batches.

The code below measures this for any PyTorch model: it takes many random batches at a fixed parameter value and reports the mean squared deviation from the full-batch gradient.

pythonmeasure_gradient_noise.py
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F

torch.manual_seed(0)
N = 300
X = torch.randn(N, 2)
y = (X[:, 0] * X[:, 1] > 0).long()           # XOR-like 2-class toy labels
model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 2))

def flat_grad(xb, yb):
    """Gradient of the mean loss on (xb, yb), flattened into one vector."""
    model.zero_grad()
    F.cross_entropy(model(xb), yb).backward()
    return torch.cat([p.grad.flatten() for p in model.parameters()]).clone()

g_full = flat_grad(X, y)                      # "true" gradient (full batch)
print(f"||G||^2 = {g_full.pow(2).sum():.4f}")

for B in [1, 4, 16, 64, 256]:
    errs = []
    for _ in range(300):
        idx = torch.randperm(N)[:B]           # sample without replacement
        errs.append((flat_grad(X[idx], y[idx]) - g_full).pow(2).sum())
    print(f"B={B:4d}  E||g_B - G||^2 = {torch.stack(errs).mean():8.4f}")

Running it you should see the error shrink roughly in proportion to 1/B1/B1/B (a little faster for BBB close to NNN, because of the finite-population correction).

The effect of batch size

If you double the batch size, each step costs about twice the compute but its gradient has half the noise variance. Whether that is a good deal depends on whether noise or curvature is the bottleneck, and the gradient noise scale makes this precise. McCandlish et al. (2018) define (in its simple form)

Bnoise=tr⁡(Σ)∥G∥2,\mathcal{B}_{\text{noise}}=\frac{\tr(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})}{\norm{\boldsymbol{G}}^2},Bnoise​=∥G∥2tr(Σ)​,

the batch size at which the noise in the gradient estimate is about as large as the signal. The qualitative prediction is a two-regime picture.

  • For B≪BnoiseB\ll\mathcal{B}_{\text{noise}}B≪Bnoise​ the gradient is mostly noise, and averaging more examples helps almost linearly: doubling BBB lets you double the learning rate and halve the number of steps for the same progress, at the same total compute. Large batches give near-perfect parallel speed-up.
  • For B≫BnoiseB\gg\mathcal{B}_{\text{noise}}B≫Bnoise​ the gradient is already accurate. More examples give a slightly better estimate and no extra progress per step: you pay twice the compute for nothing, and the number of steps stops falling. There are diminishing returns.

The noise scale is not a constant. It is small early in training, when gradients all point the same way, and grows by orders of magnitude as the loss falls and the signal ∥G∥\norm{\boldsymbol{G}}∥G∥ shrinks. This is why people use small batches or progressive batch-size growth for the early phase and why harder tasks tolerate larger batches.

Derivation: the linear scaling rule

Compare kkk consecutive SGD steps with batch size BBB and learning rate η\etaη to a single step with batch size kBkBkB and learning rate η′\eta'η′. Assume the parameters hardly move over kkk steps, so every step sees essentially the same expected gradient G\boldsymbol{G}G: θt+k≈θt−η∑j=0k−1gt+j≈θt−kη G−η∑jξj,\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+k}\approx\boldsymbol{\theta}_t-\eta\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\boldsymbol{g}_{t+j}\approx \boldsymbol{\theta}_t - k\eta\,\boldsymbol{G}-\eta\sum_j\boldsymbol{\xi}_j,θt+k​≈θt​−ηj=0∑k−1​gt+j​≈θt​−kηG−ηj∑​ξj​, where ξj\boldsymbol{\xi}_jξj​ is zero-mean noise with covariance Σ/B\boldsymbol{\Sigma}/BΣ/B. A single large-batch step gives θt−η′G−η′ξ\boldsymbol{\theta}_t-\eta'\boldsymbol{G}-\eta'\boldsymbol{\xi}θt​−η′G−η′ξ with Cov⁡[ξ]=Σ/(kB)\Cov[\boldsymbol{\xi}]=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}/(kB)Cov[ξ]=Σ/(kB). The drift terms match if η′=kη\eta'=k\etaη′=kη. The noise covariance then is η′2Σ/(kB)=kη2Σ/B\eta'^2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}/(kB)=k\eta^2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}/Bη′2Σ/(kB)=kη2Σ/B for the large batch and k η2Σ/Bk\,\eta^2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}/Bkη2Σ/B for the kkk small steps: they match as well. So: multiply the batch size by kkk, multiply the learning rate by kkk and training dynamics over the same number of epochs are approximately preserved. (With Adam the corresponding heuristic is a square-root rule, η′≈k η\eta'\approx\sqrt{k}\,\etaη′≈k​η, because the update is normalized by the gradient scale.)

The assumption that the parameters hardly move is exactly what fails at the start of training, when the weights change rapidly, and at very large batch sizes. Goyal et al. (2017) trained ResNet-50 on ImageNet with batch size 8192 using the linear scaling rule plus a gradual warmup of the learning rate during the first few epochs, and matched the accuracy of the small-batch baseline; beyond roughly this batch size they saw the accuracy degrade. The chart below reproduces the rule in miniature.

Rules of thumb for choosing a batch size

Pick the largest batch that fits in memory and keeps accelerator utilization high, scale the learning rate with it (linearly for SGD, roughly as the square root for Adam), add warmup, and verify on validation accuracy. If you cannot afford the memory, use gradient accumulation: run kkk micro-batches, sum the gradients, and call optimizer.step() once. This is mathematically the same as one batch of kBkBkB (except for BatchNorm, whose statistics are computed per micro-batch).

Momentum and Nesterov accelerated gradient

On a ravine, plain SGD oscillates across the walls (large gradient components with alternating sign) and makes slow progress along the floor (small gradient components with a consistent sign). Momentum (Polyak, 1964, "heavy ball") keeps an exponentially decaying running sum of past gradients, the velocity v\boldsymbol{v}v. Components that alternate in sign cancel in that sum; components that keep their sign accumulate.

vt=β vt−1+gt,θt=θt−1−η vt,\boldsymbol{v}_{t}=\beta\,\boldsymbol{v}_{t-1}+\boldsymbol{g}_t,\qquad \boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}=\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t-1}-\eta\,\boldsymbol{v}_{t},vt​=βvt−1​+gt​,θt​=θt−1​−ηvt​,

with β∈[0,1)\beta\in[0,1)β∈[0,1), typically 0.90.90.9. (PyTorch's SGD(momentum=...) uses exactly this form. Some texts write vt=βvt−1−ηgt\boldsymbol{v}_t=\beta\boldsymbol{v}_{t-1}-\eta\boldsymbol{g}_tvt​=βvt−1​−ηgt​ and θt=θt−1+vt\boldsymbol{\theta}_t=\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t-1}+\boldsymbol{v}_tθt​=θt−1​+vt​; the two are equivalent after rescaling v\boldsymbol{v}v by η\etaη when η\etaη is constant.) Unrolling the recursion shows that the update is −η∑s≤tβt−sgs-\eta\sum_{s\le t}\beta^{t-s}\boldsymbol{g}_s−η∑s≤t​βt−sgs​: a weighted sum of past gradients with an effective memory of about 1/(1−β)1/(1-\beta)1/(1−β) steps. For a constant gradient g\boldsymbol{g}g the velocity saturates at g/(1−β)\boldsymbol{g}/(1-\beta)g/(1−β), so momentum 0.9 gives an effective learning rate ten times larger along consistent directions. When you add momentum, you should usually lower η\etaη accordingly.

Why momentum accelerates: the quadratic case

On f=12λθ2f=\tfrac12\lambda\theta^2f=21​λθ2 (one eigendirection of a quadratic) the heavy-ball iteration in the form θt+1=θt−ηλθt+β(θt−θt−1)\theta_{t+1}=\theta_t-\eta\lambda\theta_t+\beta(\theta_t-\theta_{t-1})θt+1​=θt​−ηλθt​+β(θt​−θt−1​) is the linear recurrence θt+1=(1+β−ηλ)θt−βθt−1\theta_{t+1}=(1+\beta-\eta\lambda)\theta_t-\beta\theta_{t-1}θt+1​=(1+β−ηλ)θt​−βθt−1​. Its characteristic polynomial is z2−(1+β−ηλ)z+β=0z^2-(1+\beta-\eta\lambda)z+\beta=0z2−(1+β−ηλ)z+β=0. When the roots are complex, which happens when (1+β−ηλ)2<4β(1+\beta-\eta\lambda)^2<4\beta(1+β−ηλ)2<4β, both roots have modulus exactly β\sqrt{\beta}β​ regardless of λ\lambdaλ. So for every curvature in that range the error decays at the same rate β\sqrt\betaβ​ per step (with oscillation). The range covers all λ∈[λmin⁡,λmax⁡]\lambda\in[\lambda_{\min},\lambda_{\max}]λ∈[λmin​,λmax​] if η\etaη and β\betaβ are tuned as η=4(λmax⁡+λmin⁡)2,β=(κ−1κ+1)2,\eta=\frac{4}{(\sqrt{\lambda_{\max}}+\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}})^2},\qquad \beta=\left(\frac{\sqrt\kappa-1}{\sqrt\kappa+1}\right)^2,η=(λmax​​+λmin​​)24​,β=(κ​+1κ​−1​)2, giving a per-step rate of κ−1κ+1\frac{\sqrt\kappa-1}{\sqrt\kappa+1}κ​+1κ​−1​. Compare that with κ−1κ+1\frac{\kappa-1}{\kappa+1}κ+1κ−1​ for gradient descent: the number of iterations falls from O(κ)O(\kappa)O(κ) to O(κ)O(\sqrt\kappa)O(κ​). With κ=104\kappa=10^4κ=104 that is the difference between 10,000 and 100 steps. This is the best possible rate for any first-order method on quadratics. Real networks are not quadratics, and the tuned values are unknowable in advance, so in practice β=0.9\beta=0.9β=0.9 is simply a good default.

Nesterov accelerated gradient

Nesterov (1983) proposed a subtle change: evaluate the gradient not at the current position but at the look-ahead point where momentum alone is about to carry you.

vt=β vt−1+∇L(θt−1−ηβ vt−1),θt=θt−1−η vt.\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol{v}_{t}&=\beta\,\boldsymbol{v}_{t-1}+\nabla\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t-1}-\eta\beta\,\boldsymbol{v}_{t-1}),\\ \boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}&=\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t-1}-\eta\,\boldsymbol{v}_{t}. \end{aligned}vt​θt​​=βvt−1​+∇L(θt−1​−ηβvt−1​),=θt−1​−ηvt​.​

If the momentum step is about to overshoot, the look-ahead gradient already points back and reduces the velocity: it is a built-in brake. For smooth convex problems Nesterov's method achieves the optimal O(1/t2)O(1/t^2)O(1/t2) rate versus O(1/t)O(1/t)O(1/t) for plain gradient descent; for strongly convex quadratics the improvement over heavy ball is in the constants. In deep learning the gain is modest but consistent, and Sutskever et al. (2013) popularized it. In PyTorch, set nesterov=True, which implements a reformulation that needs only the gradient at the current iterate, so there is no extra backward pass.

pythonmomentum_from_scratch.py
import numpy as np

# Ill-conditioned quadratic f(x, y) = 0.5 * (30 x^2 + y^2); curvatures 30 and 1.
H = np.array([30.0, 1.0])
grad = lambda th: H * th
f = lambda th: 0.5 * np.sum(H * th**2)

def run(kind, lr, beta=0.9, steps=60, start=(-1.6, 1.5)):
    th = np.array(start); v = np.zeros(2); hist = [f(th)]
    for _ in range(steps):
        if kind == "sgd":
            th = th - lr * grad(th)
        elif kind == "momentum":
            v = beta * v + grad(th)
            th = th - lr * v
        elif kind == "nesterov":
            v = beta * v + grad(th - lr * beta * v)   # gradient at the look-ahead point
            th = th - lr * v
        hist.append(f(th))
    return np.array(hist)

for kind, lr in [("sgd", 0.06), ("momentum", 0.015), ("nesterov", 0.015)]:
    h = run(kind, lr)
    print(f"{kind:9s} lr={lr:<6} loss after 20 steps {h[20]:.2e}, after 60 steps {h[60]:.2e}")

Note the largest stable plain-GD step is 2/30≈0.0672/30\approx0.0672/30≈0.067, which is why the SGD run uses 0.06 and still zigzags: it contracts the steep coordinate by ∣1−0.06⋅30∣=0.8|1-0.06\cdot30|=0.8∣1−0.06⋅30∣=0.8 per step while the shallow coordinate shrinks by only 0.940.940.94 per step. Try the "Optimizer race" demo above with β=0\beta=0β=0 and β=0.9\beta=0.9β=0.9 to feel this difference.

Adaptive learning rates: AdaGrad, RMSProp, Adam, AdamW

Momentum fixes the direction but still uses one global learning rate for every parameter. In a network, different parameters live at wildly different gradient scales (embedding rows of rare words versus common words, early layers versus late layers, biases versus weights). Adaptive methods keep a per-parameter running estimate of the typical gradient magnitude and divide the step by it, so every coordinate moves at a comparable speed.

AdaGrad

Duchi, Hazan and Singer (2011) accumulate the sum of squared gradients for each coordinate:

st=st−1+gt⊙gt,θt=θt−1−ηst+ε⊙gt,\boldsymbol{s}_t=\boldsymbol{s}_{t-1}+\boldsymbol{g}_t\odot\boldsymbol{g}_t,\qquad \boldsymbol{\theta}_t=\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t-1}-\frac{\eta}{\sqrt{\boldsymbol{s}_t}+\varepsilon}\odot\boldsymbol{g}_t,st​=st−1​+gt​⊙gt​,θt​=θt−1​−st​​+εη​⊙gt​,

where ⊙\odot⊙ is elementwise multiplication and all operations on vectors are elementwise. Coordinates with large past gradients get smaller steps; rare features whose gradients are mostly zero keep a large step on the few occasions they appear. That is a wonderful property for sparse problems (bag-of-words models, embeddings). The weakness is that st\boldsymbol{s}_tst​ only grows, so the effective learning rate η/st\eta/\sqrt{s_t}η/st​​ decays monotonically, roughly like 1/t1/\sqrt{t}1/t​ in the constant-gradient case, and in non-convex deep learning training can stall long before it converges.

RMSProp

Geoffrey Hinton proposed, in a 2012 Coursera lecture (never formally published), replacing the sum by an exponential moving average so the denominator forgets old gradients:

st=ρ st−1+(1−ρ) gt⊙gt,θt=θt−1−ηst+ε⊙gt,\boldsymbol{s}_t=\rho\,\boldsymbol{s}_{t-1}+(1-\rho)\,\boldsymbol{g}_t\odot\boldsymbol{g}_t,\qquad \boldsymbol{\theta}_t=\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t-1}-\frac{\eta}{\sqrt{\boldsymbol{s}_t}+\varepsilon}\odot\boldsymbol{g}_t,st​=ρst−1​+(1−ρ)gt​⊙gt​,θt​=θt−1​−st​​+εη​⊙gt​,

with ρ≈0.9\rho\approx0.9ρ≈0.9 (or 0.99). Now st\sqrt{\boldsymbol{s}_t}st​​ approximates the recent root-mean-square (RMS) gradient per coordinate, so the update has magnitude about η\etaη per coordinate whatever the gradient scale. This is a diagonal approximation to a second-order method: dividing by the RMS gradient crudely rescales each coordinate toward unit curvature.

Adam

Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2014; ICLR 2015) combines momentum on the gradient (first moment) with RMSProp scaling (second moment), plus a bias correction:

mt=β1mt−1+(1−β1)gt,vt=β2vt−1+(1−β2) gt⊙gt,m^t=mt1−β1t,v^t=vt1−β2t,θt=θt−1−η m^tv^t+ε.\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol{m}_t&=\beta_1\boldsymbol{m}_{t-1}+(1-\beta_1)\boldsymbol{g}_t,\\ \boldsymbol{v}_t&=\beta_2\boldsymbol{v}_{t-1}+(1-\beta_2)\,\boldsymbol{g}_t\odot\boldsymbol{g}_t,\\ \hat{\boldsymbol{m}}_t&=\frac{\boldsymbol{m}_t}{1-\beta_1^t},\qquad \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_t=\frac{\boldsymbol{v}_t}{1-\beta_2^t},\\ \boldsymbol{\theta}_t&=\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t-1}-\eta\,\frac{\hat{\boldsymbol{m}}_t}{\sqrt{\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_t}+\varepsilon}. \end{aligned}mt​vt​m^t​θt​​=β1​mt−1​+(1−β1​)gt​,=β2​vt−1​+(1−β2​)gt​⊙gt​,=1−β1t​mt​​,v^t​=1−β2t​vt​​,=θt−1​−ηv^t​​+εm^t​​.​

The defaults β1=0.9\beta_1=0.9β1​=0.9, β2=0.999\beta_2=0.999β2​=0.999, ε=10−8\varepsilon=10^{-8}ε=10−8 and η=10−3\eta=10^{-3}η=10−3 are remarkably robust. The first moment m\boldsymbol{m}m averages roughly the last 10 gradients (momentum), the second moment v\boldsymbol{v}v the last 1000 (a smooth estimate of the gradient variance plus mean-square).

Derivation: why the bias correction is needed

Initialize m0=0\boldsymbol{m}_0=\mathbf{0}m0​=0. Unrolling the recursion gives mt=(1−β1)∑i=1tβ1t−igi\boldsymbol{m}_t=(1-\beta_1)\sum_{i=1}^t\beta_1^{t-i}\boldsymbol{g}_imt​=(1−β1​)∑i=1t​β1t−i​gi​. Suppose the gradients are drawn from a stationary distribution with mean μ=E[gi]\boldsymbol{\mu}=\E[\boldsymbol{g}_i]μ=E[gi​]. Then E[mt]=μ (1−β1)∑i=1tβ1t−i=μ (1−β1t).\E[\boldsymbol{m}_t]=\boldsymbol{\mu}\,(1-\beta_1)\sum_{i=1}^t\beta_1^{t-i}=\boldsymbol{\mu}\,(1-\beta_1^t).E[mt​]=μ(1−β1​)i=1∑t​β1t−i​=μ(1−β1t​). So mt\boldsymbol{m}_tmt​ is a biased (shrunk) estimate of μ\boldsymbol{\mu}μ by the factor 1−β1t1-\beta_1^t1−β1t​, which is tiny at the start (0.10.10.1 at t=1t=1t=1 for β1=0.9\beta_1=0.9β1​=0.9) and tends to 1 later. Dividing by it, m^t=mt/(1−β1t)\hat{\boldsymbol{m}}_t=\boldsymbol{m}_t/(1-\beta_1^t)m^t​=mt​/(1−β1t​), makes the estimator unbiased. For v\boldsymbol{v}v the effect is far larger: with β2=0.999\beta_2=0.999β2​=0.999 the factor is 0.0010.0010.001 at t=1t=1t=1, so without correction v1=0.001 ∣g1∣≈0.03∣g1∣\sqrt{\boldsymbol{v}_1}=\sqrt{0.001}\,|\boldsymbol{g}_1|\approx0.03|\boldsymbol{g}_1|v1​​=0.001​∣g1​∣≈0.03∣g1​∣ and the first step would be ≈30×\approx 30\times≈30× too large, since m1/v1=0.1g1/(0.032∣g1∣)≈3.2\boldsymbol{m}_1/\sqrt{\boldsymbol{v}_1}=0.1\boldsymbol{g}_1/(0.032|\boldsymbol{g}_1|)\approx3.2m1​/v1​​=0.1g1​/(0.032∣g1​∣)≈3.2. With the correction, m^1/v^1=g1/∣g1∣=±1\hat{\boldsymbol{m}}_1/\sqrt{\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_1}=\boldsymbol{g}_1/|\boldsymbol{g}_1|=\pm1m^1​/v^1​​=g1​/∣g1​∣=±1, so the first update has magnitude exactly η\etaη per coordinate. In general, with bias correction the per-coordinate step size is bounded by roughly η\etaη (up to a factor related to (1−β1)/1−β2(1-\beta_1)/\sqrt{1-\beta_2}(1−β1​)/1−β2​​ in the worst case), which is why Adam's learning rate has a direct meaning: "about how far each parameter may move per step".

Because the update is a ratio m^/v^\hat m/\sqrt{\hat v}m^/v^​ it is invariant to the overall scale of the gradient (multiply the loss by 1000 and Adam's trajectory is unchanged apart from ε\varepsilonε). It behaves like a smoothed sign descent when gradients are noisy: if the mean μ\muμ is small relative to the RMS Eg2\sqrt{\E g^2}Eg2​, the step shrinks automatically. This is a sensible signal-to-noise adaptation. Be aware of the known caveats: Reddi et al. (2018) constructed convex examples where Adam fails to converge (motivating AMSGrad), and Wilson et al. (2017) found that well-tuned SGD with momentum sometimes generalizes better than adaptive methods on image tasks. In practice Adam variants are the default for transformers, GANs, and most NLP, while SGD with momentum remains common in vision (ResNets).

pythonadam_from_scratch.py
import numpy as np

class Adam:
    """Adam (Kingma & Ba) with optional decoupled weight decay (AdamW).
    params: list of np.ndarray updated in place."""
    def __init__(self, params, lr=1e-3, betas=(0.9, 0.999), eps=1e-8,
                 weight_decay=0.0, decoupled=True):
        self.p, self.lr, (self.b1, self.b2), self.eps = params, lr, betas, eps
        self.wd, self.decoupled, self.t = weight_decay, decoupled, 0
        self.m = [np.zeros_like(q) for q in params]
        self.v = [np.zeros_like(q) for q in params]

    def step(self, grads):
        self.t += 1
        for q, g, m, v in zip(self.p, grads, self.m, self.v):
            if self.wd and not self.decoupled:
                g = g + self.wd * q                    # classic L2: goes through the adaptive scaling
            m *= self.b1; m += (1 - self.b1) * g       # first moment (in place)
            v *= self.b2; v += (1 - self.b2) * g * g   # second moment
            m_hat = m / (1 - self.b1 ** self.t)        # bias corrections
            v_hat = v / (1 - self.b2 ** self.t)
            if self.wd and self.decoupled:
                q -= self.lr * self.wd * q             # AdamW: shrink weights directly
            q -= self.lr * m_hat / (np.sqrt(v_hat) + self.eps)

# Sanity check: first step has size ~lr for every coordinate, whatever the gradient scale.
w = [np.zeros(3)]
opt = Adam(w, lr=0.1)
opt.step([np.array([1e-6, 1.0, 1e4])])
print(w[0])        # approximately [-0.1, -0.1, -0.1]

The check at the bottom shows scale invariance: gradients spanning ten orders of magnitude still produce steps of equal size, a defining property of Adam's first step. (For the 10−610^{-6}10−6 coordinate the value is slightly below 0.10.10.1 because ε=10−8\varepsilon=10^{-8}ε=10−8 is no longer negligible compared with ∣g∣|g|∣g∣.)

AdamW: decoupled weight decay

Weight decay shrinks every weight a little at each step, θ←(1−ηλ)θ\boldsymbol{\theta}\leftarrow(1-\eta\lambda)\boldsymbol{\theta}θ←(1−ηλ)θ, to keep weights small. For plain SGD this is identical to adding an ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ penalty λ2∥θ∥2\frac\lambda2\norm{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^22λ​∥θ∥2 to the loss, because the penalty's gradient is λθ\lambda\boldsymbol{\theta}λθ and the step is −η(g+λθ)-\eta(\boldsymbol{g}+\lambda\boldsymbol{\theta})−η(g+λθ). Early Adam implementations simply added λθ\lambda\boldsymbol{\theta}λθ to the gradient, because people assumed the equivalence carries over. It does not.

Why the equivalence breaks for Adam

With the ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ penalty folded into the gradient, gt′=gt+λθt−1\boldsymbol{g}_t'=\boldsymbol{g}_t+\lambda\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t-1}gt′​=gt​+λθt−1​, and the penalty term flows through both moment estimates. In the simplest case (β1=0\beta_1=0β1​=0, ignoring ε\varepsilonε) the update is Δθ=−η gt+λθvt′=−ηgtvt′−ηλθvt′.\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}=-\eta\,\frac{\boldsymbol{g}_t+\lambda\boldsymbol{\theta}}{\sqrt{\boldsymbol{v}_t'}}=-\eta\frac{\boldsymbol{g}_t}{\sqrt{\boldsymbol{v}_t'}}-\eta\lambda\frac{\boldsymbol{\theta}}{\sqrt{\boldsymbol{v}_t'}}.Δθ=−ηvt′​​gt​+λθ​=−ηvt′​​gt​​−ηλvt′​​θ​. The effective decay of coordinate jjj is ηλ/vt,j′\eta\lambda/\sqrt{v'_{t,j}}ηλ/vt,j′​​: parameters with large historical gradients (large vvv) are regularized less, while parameters with tiny gradients are regularized more. The strength of the regularizer is coupled to the gradient statistics of the loss, which has nothing to do with the intended penalty. Loshchilov and Hutter (2019) therefore decouple the two, applying the decay directly to the weights outside the adaptive pipeline: θt=θt−1−η(m^tv^t+ε+λ θt−1).\boldsymbol{\theta}_t=\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t-1}-\eta\left(\frac{\hat{\boldsymbol{m}}_t}{\sqrt{\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_t}+\varepsilon}+\lambda\,\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t-1}\right).θt​=θt−1​−η(v^t​​+εm^t​​+λθt−1​). Every weight is now shrunk by the same relative factor 1−ηλ1-\eta\lambda1−ηλ per step, independent of its gradient history. As a bonus, the best values of η\etaη and λ\lambdaλ become less entangled, which makes hyperparameter search easier. (In the paper's formulation a schedule multiplier αt\alpha_tαt​ multiplies both terms, so weight decay follows the schedule too.)

AdamW is the default optimizer for training transformers and most modern models, typically with β2\beta_2β2​ lowered to 0.950.950.95 to 0.980.980.98 for large language models and λ≈0.01\lambda\approx0.01λ≈0.01 to 0.10.10.1. Weight decay should usually be excluded from biases and normalization parameters, as in the following PyTorch snippet.

pythonadamw_param_groups.py
import torch, torch.nn as nn

model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(128, 256), nn.LayerNorm(256), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(256, 10))

decay, no_decay = [], []
for name, p in model.named_parameters():
    if not p.requires_grad:
        continue
    # biases and 1-D parameters (LayerNorm/BatchNorm gain and shift) are not decayed
    (no_decay if p.ndim < 2 else decay).append(p)

optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(
    [{"params": decay, "weight_decay": 0.05},
     {"params": no_decay, "weight_decay": 0.0}],
    lr=3e-4, betas=(0.9, 0.999), eps=1e-8)

print([len(g["params"]) for g in optimizer.param_groups])   # [2, 3]: two weight matrices; two biases + LN gain/shift
Where these methods came from

Momentum for optimization is due to Boris Polyak (1964); Yurii Nesterov's look-ahead method followed in 1983. AdaGrad (2011) was motivated by online learning and sparse features. RMSProp appeared in Hinton's 2012 Coursera lecture and was adopted everywhere without ever being written up as a paper. Adam was posted to arXiv in December 2014 (ICLR 2015) and became one of the most cited papers in machine learning. AdamW (arXiv 2017, ICLR 2019) fixed a subtle but important flaw that had been silently hurting regularization for years.

Learning-rate schedules

The learning rate is the most important hyperparameter, and a constant value is almost never optimal. Early in training you want to move fast, late in training you want to settle into a minimum without bouncing around due to gradient noise. In the continuous-time picture, the stationary spread of the iterates around a minimum scales with η/B\eta/Bη/B, so decaying η\etaη is a way to shrink the noise ball and sharpen the final answer, which is why a sudden improvement in loss appears every time the learning rate drops.

Before looking at specific schedules, here is why a schedule helps at all. Near a minimum with SGD noise, the stationary spread of the iterates scales roughly with η/B\eta/Bη/B (see the noise argument in the batch-size section): a large constant rate keeps the loss floating above the floor set by the noise. Decaying η\etaη shrinks the noise ball and lets the model settle. Early on the opposite problem holds: you want the largest stable rate to move quickly through the flat, high-loss regions.

The standard schedules

Write η0\eta_0η0​ for the base (peak) rate, ttt for the step and TTT for the total number of steps.

  • Step decay. ηt=η0 γ⌊t/s⌋\eta_t=\eta_0\,\gamma^{\lfloor t/s\rfloor}ηt​=η0​γ⌊t/s⌋: multiply by γ\gammaγ (commonly 0.10.10.1) every sss steps. The classic ImageNet recipe drops the rate by 10x at epochs 30, 60 and 90. Simple and still competitive, but the drop points are two extra hyperparameters.
  • Cosine annealing (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017). ηt=ηmin⁡+12(η0−ηmin⁡)(1+cos⁡(πt/T))\eta_t=\eta_{\min}+\tfrac12(\eta_0-\eta_{\min})\big(1+\cos(\pi t/T)\big)ηt​=ηmin​+21​(η0​−ηmin​)(1+cos(πt/T)). It decays slowly at first, fastest in the middle, and gently toward the end, and needs only TTT. This is the dominant choice for modern vision and language training. (The original SGDR variant restarts the cosine periodically.)
  • Linear warmup. ηt=η0 t/Tw\eta_t=\eta_0\,t/T_wηt​=η0​t/Tw​ for t<Twt<T_wt<Tw​, usually followed by one of the decays above. Warmup is needed because at initialization the loss surface is at its sharpest and Adam's second-moment estimate is built from very few samples; a full-size step at t=0t=0t=0 can throw the weights into a region from which training never recovers. Transformers essentially always need it (a few hundred to a few thousand steps), and large-batch SGD needs it too (Goyal et al., 2017).
  • Cyclical learning rates (Smith, 2017). The rate oscillates between ηmin⁡\eta_{\min}ηmin​ and ηmax⁡\eta_{\max}ηmax​, e.g. triangularly with half-period sss: ηt=ηmin⁡+(ηmax⁡−ηmin⁡)max⁡ ⁣(0, 1−∣t/s−2k−1∣)\eta_t=\eta_{\min}+(\eta_{\max}-\eta_{\min})\max\!\big(0,\,1-|t/s-2k-1|\big)ηt​=ηmin​+(ηmax​−ηmin​)max(0,1−∣t/s−2k−1∣) with k=⌊t/(2s)⌋k=\lfloor t/(2s)\rfloork=⌊t/(2s)⌋. Periodically raising the rate helps cross saddles and flat regions; Smith also proposed the LR range test: sweep the rate exponentially upward during one short run and pick the range where the loss falls fastest.
  • One-cycle policy (Smith and Topin, 2018, "super-convergence"). One triangle: warm up from η0/25\eta_0/25η0​/25 (say) to a large peak over about 30 percent of training, then anneal (linearly or by cosine) to a rate far below the start, often 10−410^{-4}10−4 of the peak. Together with momentum cycled in the opposite direction, it can train some networks in a fraction of the usual epochs. PyTorch ships it as OneCycleLR.
InteractiveLearning-rate schedules: shape, warmup and the area under the curve

All of these are a few lines of code. The version below returns a multiplier on the base rate, which is exactly what torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LambdaLR expects.

pythonlr_schedules.py
import math

def warmup_cosine(step, total, warmup, min_ratio=0.0):
    """LR multiplier: linear warmup for `warmup` steps, then cosine decay to min_ratio."""
    if step < warmup:
        return (step + 1) / warmup                       # never exactly 0, so the first step moves
    progress = (step - warmup) / max(1, total - warmup)  # 0 -> 1
    return min_ratio + 0.5 * (1 - min_ratio) * (1 + math.cos(math.pi * progress))

def step_decay(step, every, gamma=0.1):
    return gamma ** (step // every)

def triangular(step, half_period, lo=0.1):
    cycle = step // (2 * half_period)
    x = abs(step / half_period - 2 * cycle - 1)           # 1 -> 0 -> 1 within a cycle
    return lo + (1 - lo) * max(0.0, 1 - x)

T = 1000
for t in [0, 50, 99, 100, 300, 600, 999]:
    print(f"t={t:4d}  warmup+cosine {warmup_cosine(t, T, 100):.3f}  step {step_decay(t, 300):.3f}  tri {triangular(t, 100):.3f}")

# Using it in PyTorch (sketch):
#   opt   = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=3e-4)
#   sched = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LambdaLR(opt, lambda s: warmup_cosine(s, T, 100))
#   ... each iteration:  opt.step(); sched.step()          # step the scheduler per iteration, not per epoch
Choosing a schedule

Default to linear warmup followed by cosine decay (to about 10 percent of peak or to zero) and pick the peak rate with a quick LR range test. Make the schedule a function of the total number of steps, so changing the training length rescales the whole curve. If you stop a cosine run early you stop at a large learning rate and the result is poor: decide the budget first.

Weight initialization

A network's first gradient step is determined entirely by its initial weights, and so is whether the signal survives the trip through dozens of layers. Initialization is therefore not a detail. The principle is simple: choose the weight variance so that the scale of activations (forward) and of gradients (backward) stays roughly constant from layer to layer. If each layer multiplies the variance by 2 the signal grows as 2L2^L2L; by 12\tfrac1221​, it shrinks as 2−L2^{-L}2−L. At L=30L=30L=30 that is a factor of a billion either way.

Deriving Xavier/Glorot initialization

Consider a dense layer zj=∑i=1ninwijaiz_j=\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\rm in}}w_{ij}a_izj​=∑i=1nin​​wij​ai​ (ignore the bias, initialized at 0), with a=ϕ(zprev)a=\phi(z_{\rm prev})a=ϕ(zprev​). Assume the weights are i.i.d. with mean 0 and variance σw2\sigma_w^2σw2​, independent of the inputs, and that the inputs aia_iai​ are i.i.d.

Forward variance

Because the terms are independent and zero-mean, Var⁡(zj)=∑i=1ninVar⁡(wijai)=nin σw2 E[ai2].\Var(z_j)=\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\rm in}}\Var(w_{ij}a_i)=n_{\rm in}\,\sigma_w^2\,\E[a_i^2].Var(zj​)=i=1∑nin​​Var(wij​ai​)=nin​σw2​E[ai2​]. Here we used E[wijai]=0\E[w_{ij}a_i]=0E[wij​ai​]=0 and Var⁡(wijai)=E[w2]E[a2]\Var(w_{ij}a_i)=\E[w^2]\E[a^2]Var(wij​ai​)=E[w2]E[a2]. For a symmetric activation that is approximately linear near zero (tanh, or no activation), E[a2]≈Var⁡(zprev)\E[a^2]\approx\Var(z_{\rm prev})E[a2]≈Var(zprev​), so to keep the variance constant from layer to layer we need nin σw2=1.n_{\rm in}\,\sigma_w^2=1.nin​σw2​=1.

Backward variance

In the backward pass the gradient with respect to a layer's input is aˉi=∑j=1noutwijzˉj\bar a_i=\sum_{j=1}^{n_{\rm out}}w_{ij}\bar z_jaˉi​=∑j=1nout​​wij​zˉj​, a sum of noutn_{\rm out}nout​ terms. The same computation gives Var⁡(aˉi)=nout σw2 Var⁡(zˉ)\Var(\bar a_i)=n_{\rm out}\,\sigma_w^2\,\Var(\bar z)Var(aˉi​)=nout​σw2​Var(zˉ) (taking ϕ′≈1\phi'\approx1ϕ′≈1), so keeping gradient variance constant needs nout σw2=1.n_{\rm out}\,\sigma_w^2=1.nout​σw2​=1.

When nin≠noutn_{\rm in}\neq n_{\rm out}nin​=nout​ we cannot satisfy both. Glorot and Bengio (2010) split the difference with the harmonic compromise

σw2=2nin+nout,i.e. Wij∼N ⁣(0,2nin+nout)  or  Unif ⁣[−a,a], a=6nin+nout.\sigma_w^2=\frac{2}{n_{\rm in}+n_{\rm out}},\qquad\text{i.e. } W_{ij}\sim\mathcal N\!\Big(0,\tfrac{2}{n_{\rm in}+n_{\rm out}}\Big)\ \text{ or }\ \mathrm{Unif}\!\big[-a,a\big],\ a=\sqrt{\tfrac{6}{n_{\rm in}+n_{\rm out}}}.σw2​=nin​+nout​2​,i.e. Wij​∼N(0,nin​+nout​2​)  or  Unif[−a,a], a=nin​+nout​6​​.

(The uniform bound follows from Var⁡(Unif[−a,a])=a2/3\Var(\mathrm{Unif}[-a,a])=a^2/3Var(Unif[−a,a])=a2/3.) This is nn.init.xavier_normal_ / xavier_uniform_. LeCun's earlier rule σw2=1/nin\sigma_w^2=1/n_{\rm in}σw2​=1/nin​ matches the forward condition only.

Deriving He (Kaiming) initialization

ReLU breaks the "approximately linear" assumption: it zeroes half the pre-activations. If zzz is symmetric around zero, then E[ReLU⁡(z)2]=12E[z2]=12Var⁡(z)\E[\relu(z)^2]=\tfrac12\E[z^2]=\tfrac12\Var(z)E[ReLU(z)2]=21​E[z2]=21​Var(z). Redoing the forward computation:

He variance

Var⁡(zj)=nin σw2 E[a2]=nin σw2⋅12Var⁡(zprev).\Var(z_j)=n_{\rm in}\,\sigma_w^2\,\E[a^2]=n_{\rm in}\,\sigma_w^2\cdot\tfrac12\Var(z_{\rm prev}).Var(zj​)=nin​σw2​E[a2]=nin​σw2​⋅21​Var(zprev​). Constant variance requires 12ninσw2=1\tfrac12 n_{\rm in}\sigma_w^2=121​nin​σw2​=1, that is σw2=2nin.\sigma_w^2=\frac{2}{n_{\rm in}}.σw2​=nin​2​. The same argument applies backward (only half the units pass gradient), giving 2/nout2/n_{\rm out}2/nout​; He et al. (2015) show that either choice keeps the product over layers bounded, and use ninn_{\rm in}nin​ ("fan-in" mode) by default.

Here is that effect measured. The chart shows the activation standard deviation per layer in a 30-layer network for several choices:

InteractiveInitialization explorer: activations and gradients versus depth
pythoninit_check.py
import torch, torch.nn as nn

def activation_stds(init, act, depth=30, width=256, batch=512):
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    x, stds = torch.randn(batch, width), []
    for _ in range(depth):
        lin = nn.Linear(width, width, bias=False)
        init(lin.weight)
        x = act(lin(x))
        stds.append(x.std().item())
    return stds

he = lambda w: nn.init.kaiming_normal_(w, nonlinearity="relu")   # std = sqrt(2 / fan_in)
glorot = lambda w: nn.init.xavier_normal_(w)                      # std = sqrt(2 / (fan_in + fan_out))
naive = lambda w: nn.init.normal_(w, 0.0, 0.05)

for name, init, act in [("relu + He", he, torch.relu), ("relu + naive 0.05", naive, torch.relu),
                        ("tanh + Glorot", glorot, torch.tanh), ("tanh + naive 0.05", naive, torch.tanh)]:
    s = activation_stds(init, act)
    print(f"{name:20s} layer 1: {s[0]:.2e}   layer 10: {s[9]:.2e}   layer 30: {s[29]:.2e}")

Practical defaults: He for ReLU-family layers, Glorot for tanh/sigmoid/linear, biases at zero, and for transformers a small normal (std about 0.02) with residual-branch outputs scaled down by 1/2L1/\sqrt{2L}1/2L​ so that the sum of many residual contributions does not grow with depth. PyTorch's nn.Linear default is a Kaiming-uniform with a=5a=\sqrt5a=5​, which amounts to variance 1/(3nin)1/(3n_{\rm in})1/(3nin​), deliberately conservative; it is fine for shallow nets but means the default is not He. Initialization derivations assume the layer inputs are roughly independent and zero-mean; normalization layers (below) make training far less sensitive to these choices.

Vanishing and exploding gradients

Week 2 showed that the gradient reaching layer kkk is a product of per-layer Jacobians ∏ℓ>kdiag⁡(ϕ′(zℓ))Wℓ⊤\prod_{\ell>k}\diag(\phi'(\boldsymbol z_\ell))\mathbf W_\ell^\top∏ℓ>k​diag(ϕ′(zℓ​))Wℓ⊤​. The norm of a product of LLL matrices tends to grow or shrink exponentially in LLL, governed by the typical singular value ρ\rhoρ of each factor: the gradient scales like ρL−k\rho^{L-k}ρL−k. If ρ<1\rho<1ρ<1 the early layers get no learning signal (vanishing); if ρ>1\rho>1ρ>1 the gradient blows up and a single step can destroy the model (exploding).

Where each comes from:

  • Saturating activations. σ′≤0.25\sigma'\le0.25σ′≤0.25 and tanh⁡′→0\tanh'\to0tanh′→0 in the tails give factors below 1 (Hochreiter 1991; Bengio, Simard and Frasconi 1994).
  • Bad initialization. Weight variance too small shrinks signals; too large inflates them and also saturates sigmoid/tanh units.
  • Depth and recurrence. In an RNN the same W\mathbf WW is applied at every time step, so the product is WT\mathbf W^TWT and its behavior is set by the largest eigenvalue: above 1 explodes, below 1 vanishes (see Week 7).

How to diagnose it: log the gradient norm of each parameter group per step. A healthy network has comparable relative gradient magnitudes (∥g∥/∥θ∥\norm{g}/\norm{\theta}∥g∥/∥θ∥ around 10−310^{-3}10−3) across layers. Gradient norms that spike by orders of magnitude, or nan, indicate explosion; first-layer norms many orders below the last layer's indicate vanishing (compare the bar chart in Week 2).

The toolbox, in order of impact: proper initialization; non-saturating activations (ReLU family, GELU); normalization layers; residual connections (the identity path gives a Jacobian factor near 1, which is why ResNets train at depth 100+, Week 5); gated recurrent cells (LSTM/GRU); and, for explosions, gradient clipping.

Gradient clipping

Clipping bounds the size of an update without changing its direction. Two forms:

  • Clip by value: clamp each component to [−c,c][-c,c][−c,c]. Cheap but distorts the direction.
  • Clip by global norm (Pascanu, Mikolov and Bengio, 2013): treat all gradients as one vector g\boldsymbol gg and rescale

g←g⋅min⁡ ⁣(1, c∥g∥2).\boldsymbol g\leftarrow\boldsymbol g\cdot\min\!\Big(1,\ \frac{c}{\norm{\boldsymbol g}_2}\Big).g←g⋅min(1, ∥g∥2​c​).

If ∥g∥≤c\norm{\boldsymbol g}\le c∥g∥≤c nothing happens; otherwise the update has norm exactly ccc. A good threshold is a little above the typical gradient norm (log it for a few hundred steps and use something like the 90th percentile); c=1.0c=1.0c=1.0 is the near-universal default for transformers and RNNs. Clipping is a safety net against rare spikes, not a cure for a learning rate that is too high: if clipping is active on most steps the effective learning rate is simply c/∥g∥c/\norm{g}c/∥g∥ times smaller, and you should lower η\etaη instead.

pythongrad_clipping.py
import torch, torch.nn as nn

torch.manual_seed(0)
model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(10, 32), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(32, 1))
opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1)
x, y = torch.randn(64, 10), torch.randn(64, 1)
y[0] += 500.0                                     # one corrupted target: an outlier-driven gradient spike

for step in range(3):
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss = nn.functional.mse_loss(model(x), y)
    loss.backward()
    # returns the norm BEFORE clipping; use it for logging
    total_norm = nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)
    after = torch.sqrt(sum(p.grad.pow(2).sum() for p in model.parameters()))
    print(f"step {step}: loss {loss.item():9.2f}  grad norm before {total_norm:9.2f}  after {after:.2f}")
    opt.step()

Remember that with Adam, clipping interacts with the second-moment estimate (clipped gradients feed vtv_tvt​), and that clipping must happen after backward() and before optimizer.step(). With mixed precision and gradient scaling, call scaler.unscale_(optimizer) first so you clip the true gradients.

Normalization layers

Initialization sets the scale of activations at step 0, but nothing keeps it there as the weights change. Normalization layers fix this by explicitly standardizing activations inside the network. They are among the most effective training aids ever found: they allow learning rates several times larger, reduce sensitivity to initialization and make very deep networks trainable.

Batch normalization

Ioffe and Szegedy (2015) normalize each feature using the statistics of the current mini-batch. For a layer output X∈RB×C\mathbf X\in\R^{B\times C}X∈RB×C (for images, B×C×H×WB\times C\times H\times WB×C×H×W with statistics taken over B,H,WB,H,WB,H,W for each channel):

μc=1B∑nxnc,σc2=1B∑n(xnc−μc)2,x^nc=xnc−μcσc2+ε,ync=γc x^nc+βc.\mu_c=\frac1B\sum_{n}x_{nc},\qquad \sigma_c^2=\frac1B\sum_n(x_{nc}-\mu_c)^2,\qquad \hat x_{nc}=\frac{x_{nc}-\mu_c}{\sqrt{\sigma_c^2+\varepsilon}},\qquad y_{nc}=\gamma_c\,\hat x_{nc}+\beta_c .μc​=B1​n∑​xnc​,σc2​=B1​n∑​(xnc​−μc​)2,x^nc​=σc2​+ε​xnc​−μc​​,ync​=γc​x^nc​+βc​.

The learnable γc,βc\gamma_c,\beta_cγc​,βc​ let the network undo the normalization if that is best (so no expressive power is lost). Typically BN sits between the linear layer and the nonlinearity (original paper) or after the nonlinearity; both work, and with ReLU the former is the convention.

Train versus eval. During training the statistics come from the current batch, which makes each output depend on the other examples in the batch (a mild source of noise that also regularizes). At test time you want a deterministic function of one input, so BN uses running averages of the training means and variances, updated as μrun←(1−m)μrun+m μbatch\mu_{\rm run}\leftarrow(1-m)\mu_{\rm run}+m\,\mu_{\rm batch}μrun​←(1−m)μrun​+mμbatch​ with momentum m=0.1m=0.1m=0.1 in PyTorch. Forgetting model.eval() is the classic BN bug.

Backward pass of BatchNorm

Let yˉ\bar yyˉ​ denote ∂L/∂y\partial\mathcal L/\partial y∂L/∂y for one channel, and s=1/σ2+εs=1/\sqrt{\sigma^2+\varepsilon}s=1/σ2+ε​. Then γˉ=∑nyˉnx^n\bar\gamma=\sum_n\bar y_n\hat x_nγˉ​=∑n​yˉ​n​x^n​, βˉ=∑nyˉn\bar\beta=\sum_n\bar y_nβˉ​=∑n​yˉ​n​ and x^ˉn=γyˉn\bar{\hat x}_n=\gamma\bar y_nx^ˉn​=γyˉ​n​. Since every xnx_nxn​ affects x^m\hat x_mx^m​ for all mmm through μ\muμ and σ2\sigma^2σ2, three paths contribute:

  • directly: x^ˉn s\bar{\hat x}_n\,sx^ˉn​s;
  • through μ\muμ: ∂μ/∂xn=1/B\partial\mu/\partial x_n=1/B∂μ/∂xn​=1/B and ∂x^m/∂μ=−s\partial\hat x_m/\partial\mu=-s∂x^m​/∂μ=−s (plus a term through σ2\sigma^2σ2 that vanishes because ∑m(xm−μ)=0\sum_m(x_m-\mu)=0∑m​(xm​−μ)=0), giving −sB∑mx^ˉm-\frac sB\sum_m\bar{\hat x}_m−Bs​∑m​x^ˉm​;
  • through σ2\sigma^2σ2: ∂σ2/∂xn=2B(xn−μ)\partial\sigma^2/\partial x_n=\tfrac2B(x_n-\mu)∂σ2/∂xn​=B2​(xn​−μ) and ∂x^m/∂σ2=−12(xm−μ)s3\partial\hat x_m/\partial\sigma^2=-\tfrac12(x_m-\mu)s^3∂x^m​/∂σ2=−21​(xm​−μ)s3, giving −sBx^n∑mx^ˉmx^m-\frac sB\hat x_n\sum_m\bar{\hat x}_m\hat x_m−Bs​x^n​∑m​x^ˉm​x^m​.

Adding the three terms, xˉn=sB(B x^ˉn−∑mx^ˉm−x^n∑mx^ˉmx^m).\bar x_n=\frac{s}{B}\Big(B\,\bar{\hat x}_n-\sum_m\bar{\hat x}_m-\hat x_n\sum_m\bar{\hat x}_m\hat x_m\Big).xˉn​=Bs​(Bx^ˉn​−m∑​x^ˉm​−x^n​m∑​x^ˉm​x^m​). The gradient is the incoming gradient with its batch mean removed and its component along x^\hat xx^ removed: BN projects out the two directions (shift and scale) along which the output cannot change.

pythonbatchnorm_numpy.py
import numpy as np

class BatchNorm1d:
    """BatchNorm for (B, C) inputs: normalize each feature over the batch, then scale and shift."""
    def __init__(self, C, momentum=0.1, eps=1e-5):
        self.gamma, self.beta = np.ones(C), np.zeros(C)
        self.run_mean, self.run_var = np.zeros(C), np.ones(C)
        self.mom, self.eps = momentum, eps

    def forward(self, x, train=True):
        if train:
            mu, var = x.mean(axis=0), x.var(axis=0)             # biased variance (divide by B)
            self.run_mean = (1 - self.mom) * self.run_mean + self.mom * mu
            self.run_var = (1 - self.mom) * self.run_var + self.mom * var * len(x) / (len(x) - 1)  # unbiased for running
        else:
            mu, var = self.run_mean, self.run_var               # eval: fixed statistics
        self.inv_std = 1.0 / np.sqrt(var + self.eps)
        self.xhat = (x - mu) * self.inv_std
        return self.gamma * self.xhat + self.beta

    def backward(self, dy):
        B = len(dy)
        self.dgamma = (dy * self.xhat).sum(axis=0)
        self.dbeta = dy.sum(axis=0)
        dxhat = dy * self.gamma
        # compact form: dx = inv_std/B * (B*dxhat - sum(dxhat) - xhat * sum(dxhat * xhat))
        return self.inv_std / B * (B * dxhat - dxhat.sum(axis=0) - self.xhat * (dxhat * self.xhat).sum(axis=0))

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.normal(2.0, 3.0, (8, 5)); w = rng.normal(size=(8, 5))      # w makes the scalar "loss" non-trivial
bn = BatchNorm1d(5); bn.gamma = rng.normal(size=5); bn.beta = rng.normal(size=5)
loss = lambda x_: (bn.forward(x_) * w).sum()
bn.forward(x); dx = bn.backward(w)                                  # upstream gradient of that loss is w
num = np.zeros_like(x)
for i in np.ndindex(*x.shape):                                      # centered finite differences
    xp, xm = x.copy(), x.copy(); xp[i] += 1e-6; xm[i] -= 1e-6
    num[i] = (loss(xp) - loss(xm)) / 2e-6
print("max |analytic - numeric| =", np.abs(dx - num).max())        # about 1e-9

Why does it help? The original explanation, "reducing internal covariate shift" (the input distribution of each layer drifting as earlier layers change), is intuitive but was challenged: Santurkar et al. (2018) showed that injecting noise to restore covariate shift after BN does not remove the benefit, and argued that BN instead makes the loss landscape smoother (smaller Lipschitz constants of loss and gradients), which allows larger steps. A complementary view: BN makes the layer output invariant to the scale of the incoming weights, so the effective learning rate adapts automatically (the weight norm grows, the effective step shrinks; see Arora et al., 2019, and the reading list). Treat the covariate-shift story as historical motivation and the smoothing/scale-invariance story as the better-supported mechanism. What is not in dispute is the practical effect.

When BN fails. It needs reasonably large batches (with B=2B=2B=2 the statistics are mostly noise), it behaves differently in train and eval, it couples the examples in a batch (a problem for contrastive losses and for metric learning if statistics leak across samples), and it is awkward for sequence models with variable lengths. These problems motivate the alternatives.

Layer normalization

Ba, Kiros and Hinton (2016) normalize over the features of a single example, so nothing depends on the batch: μn=1C∑cxnc\mu_n=\frac1C\sum_c x_{nc}μn​=C1​∑c​xnc​, σn2=1C∑c(xnc−μn)2\sigma_n^2=\frac1C\sum_c(x_{nc}-\mu_n)^2σn2​=C1​∑c​(xnc​−μn​)2, followed by a per-feature gain and bias. Train and eval behave identically, and it works for any batch size, including 1, and for sequences. It is the standard in transformers (Week 9), where it is applied per token over the model dimension. RMSNorm (Zhang and Sennrich, 2019) drops the mean subtraction and divides only by the root-mean-square, x/1C∑cxc2+ε⋅gx/\sqrt{\frac1C\sum_c x_c^2+\varepsilon}\cdot gx/C1​∑c​xc2​+ε​⋅g, which is a little cheaper and used in many recent large language models.

Group normalization

Wu and He (2018) split the CCC channels into GGG groups and normalize within each group, per sample. G=1G=1G=1 recovers LayerNorm (over all of C,H,WC,H,WC,H,W), G=CG=CG=C recovers InstanceNorm. With G=32G=32G=32 it matches BN at large batch sizes and, unlike BN, does not degrade with batch size 2 or 4; it is the usual choice for detection and segmentation with large images and tiny batches, and for generative models.

Normalizer Statistics over Batch-dependent? Typical home
BatchNorm batch and spatial positions, per channel yes (and train/eval differ) CNNs with large batches
LayerNorm all features of one sample (one token) no Transformers, RNNs
GroupNorm channel groups of one sample no Small-batch vision, diffusion U-Nets
InstanceNorm one channel of one sample no Style transfer
RMSNorm features of one sample, no centering no Modern LLMs
InteractiveNormalization explorer: which statistics each method uses
pythonnorm_layers.py
import torch, torch.nn as nn

x = torch.randn(8, 32, 14, 14) * 3 + 5               # (N, C, H, W) with non-zero mean and large scale

for name, layer in [("BatchNorm2d", nn.BatchNorm2d(32)),
                    ("LayerNorm  ", nn.LayerNorm([32, 14, 14])),
                    ("GroupNorm  ", nn.GroupNorm(8, 32))]:
    y = layer(x)
    # BN: each channel ~ N(0,1) over (N,H,W). LN/GN: each sample (or group) ~ N(0,1) over its own axes.
    print(name, "per-channel mean (c=0):", y[:, 0].mean().item(), " per-sample mean (n=0):", y[0].mean().item())

bn = nn.BatchNorm2d(32)
bn.train(); _ = bn(x)                                  # updates running_mean / running_var
print("running_mean[0] after one batch (momentum 0.1 -> ~0.1 * 5):", bn.running_mean[0].item())
bn.eval()
y1 = bn(x[:1]); y2 = bn(x[:1])                         # eval: deterministic, no dependence on other samples
print("eval is deterministic:", torch.equal(y1, y2))

Lab: compare SGD, momentum and Adam

The lab turns every idea of the week into a controlled experiment, in pure NumPy so you can see every line. We train the same 2-64-64-3 ReLU network (the one from Week 2) on a three-arm spiral with mini-batches of 64, change one thing at a time, and read the loss curves. Everything below, including the numbers and charts, is produced by this code.

pythonoptimizer_lab.py
import numpy as np, json

def make_spiral(n=200, k=3, noise=0.2, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X, y = [], []
    for c in range(k):
        r = np.linspace(0.05, 1, n); t = np.linspace(c * 4, (c + 1) * 4, n) + rng.normal(0, noise, n)
        X.append(np.c_[r * np.sin(t), r * np.cos(t)]); y += [c] * n
    return np.vstack(X), np.array(y)

def init_params(sizes, scheme, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    Ws, bs = [], []
    for m, n in zip(sizes[:-1], sizes[1:]):
        std = {"he": np.sqrt(2 / m), "glorot": np.sqrt(2 / (m + n)),
               "small": 0.01, "large": 1.0}[scheme]
        Ws.append(rng.normal(0, std, (m, n))); bs.append(np.zeros(n))
    return Ws + bs                                   # flat list: weights then biases

def loss_and_grads(P, X, y):
    L = len(P) // 2; W, b = P[:L], P[L:]
    A = [X]; Z = []
    for l in range(L):
        Z.append(A[-1] @ W[l] + b[l]); A.append(np.maximum(Z[-1], 0) if l < L - 1 else Z[-1])
    s = A[-1] - A[-1].max(1, keepdims=True); p = np.exp(s); p /= p.sum(1, keepdims=True)
    loss = -np.log(p[np.arange(len(y)), y] + 1e-12).mean()
    d = p.copy(); d[np.arange(len(y)), y] -= 1; d /= len(y)
    gW, gb = [None] * L, [None] * L
    for l in reversed(range(L)):
        gW[l] = A[l].T @ d; gb[l] = d.sum(0)
        if l > 0: d = (d @ W[l].T) * (Z[l - 1] > 0)
    return loss, gW + gb

class SGD:
    def __init__(self, P, lr, momentum=0.0): self.P, self.lr, self.mu = P, lr, momentum; self.v = [np.zeros_like(p) for p in P]
    def step(self, G):
        for p, g, v in zip(self.P, G, self.v):
            v *= self.mu; v += g; p -= self.lr * v

class Adam:
    def __init__(self, P, lr=1e-3, b1=0.9, b2=0.999, eps=1e-8):
        self.P, self.lr, self.b1, self.b2, self.eps, self.t = P, lr, b1, b2, eps, 0
        self.m = [np.zeros_like(p) for p in P]; self.v = [np.zeros_like(p) for p in P]
    def step(self, G):
        self.t += 1
        for p, g, m, v in zip(self.P, G, self.m, self.v):
            m *= self.b1; m += (1 - self.b1) * g; v *= self.b2; v += (1 - self.b2) * g * g
            p -= self.lr * (m / (1 - self.b1 ** self.t)) / (np.sqrt(v / (1 - self.b2 ** self.t)) + self.eps)

def run(make_opt, scheme="he", epochs=60, bs=64, seed=0):
    X, y = make_spiral(); P = init_params([2, 64, 64, 3], scheme, seed); opt = make_opt(P)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed); curve = []
    for ep in range(epochs):
        perm = rng.permutation(len(X)); tot = 0.0
        for i in range(0, len(X), bs):
            idx = perm[i:i + bs]; loss, G = loss_and_grads(P, X[idx], y[idx]); opt.step(G); tot += loss * len(idx)
        curve.append(tot / len(X))
    return curve

Now the three experiments.

pythonrun_lab.py
# Experiment 1: three optimizers, same init and data order.
runs = {
    "SGD lr 0.05":          run(lambda P: SGD(P, 0.05)),
    "SGD+momentum lr 0.05": run(lambda P: SGD(P, 0.05, momentum=0.9)),
    "Adam lr 0.003":        run(lambda P: Adam(P, 0.003)),
}
for k, c in runs.items():
    print(f"{k:22s} epoch 1: {c[0]:.3f}   epoch 10: {c[9]:.3f}   epoch 30: {c[29]:.3f}   epoch 60: {c[59]:.3f}")

# Experiment 2: initialization (SGD + momentum)
for scheme in ["he", "glorot", "small", "large"]:
    c = run(lambda P: SGD(P, 0.05, momentum=0.9), scheme=scheme)
    print(f"{scheme:7s} epoch 1: {c[0]:.3f}  epoch 10: {c[9]:.3f}  epoch 60: {c[59]:.3f}")

# Experiment 3: learning-rate sweep on a log grid
for lr in [0.0003, 0.001, 0.003, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1.0]:
    print(f"lr {lr:<7} momentum: {run(lambda P: SGD(P, lr, 0.9), epochs=30)[-1]:.4f}   adam: {run(lambda P: Adam(P, lr), epochs=30)[-1]:.4f}")

Typical output (one seed, so exact digits will differ across machines only in the last digits):

text
SGD lr 0.05            epoch 1: 1.006   epoch 10: 0.630   epoch 30: 0.321   epoch 60: 0.126
SGD+momentum lr 0.05   epoch 1: 0.914   epoch 10: 0.085   epoch 30: 0.017   epoch 60: 0.006
Adam lr 0.003          epoch 1: 0.896   epoch 10: 0.224   epoch 30: 0.020   epoch 60: 0.005
he      epoch 1: 0.914  epoch 10: 0.085  epoch 60: 0.006
