Reading the optimizer curves. Plain SGD needs the steepest-direction-limited learning rate, so progress along the shallow directions is slow; momentum at the same rate (an effective rate of η/(1−β)=0.5\eta/(1-\beta)=0.5η/(1−β)=0.5) is about 20x lower in loss by epoch 30. Adam starts slower here (its bias-corrected steps are small per coordinate with η=0.003\eta=0.003η=0.003) but catches up and matches momentum by epoch 60. Neither is universally better: SGD with momentum plus a tuned schedule remains the standard for many CNN recipes, Adam(W) for transformers. Compare optimizers at their own best learning rates, never at one shared value, or you are measuring your choice of rate.

Reading the initialization curves. Initialization changes the first epochs, not the destination: Glorot lags He slightly on a ReLU net (its variance is half as large), and a weight std of 0.01 leaves the network on a plateau at the chance loss ln⁡3≈1.10\ln3\approx1.10ln3≈1.10 because the signal is too small to produce useful gradients, until it eventually breaks symmetry. The std-1 run is an honest surprise: it starts with a huge loss but trains fine in a 3-layer ReLU network, since ReLU is scale-equivariant and there is no saturation. The failure of bad initialization is a depth phenomenon (see the 30-layer chart above), which a shallow lab only hints at; try init_params([2] + [64] * 12 + [3], ...) to see it bite.

Reading the sweep. The usable learning-rate window is a band, not a point, and its position differs by optimizer. This is why the first thing to do on a new problem is a coarse log-spaced learning-rate sweep, and why the LR range test of the schedules section is worth the five minutes.

Lab extensions
  1. Add Nesterov momentum and RMSProp classes and add them to experiment 1. 2. Add gradient clipping at norm 1.0 and rerun with the lr-1.0 SGD run: does it survive? 3. Add a warmup+cosine schedule to Adam and compare final loss at lr 0.01. 4. Replace the data with a 12-layer MLP and rerun experiment 2. 5. Re-implement experiment 1 in PyTorch with torch.optim.SGD(momentum=0.9) and torch.optim.Adam and confirm you get qualitatively the same curves.

The PyTorch version of the comparison is short; here it is, so you can transfer the experiment to your own model:

pythonoptimizer_lab_torch.py
import torch, torch.nn as nn, numpy as np

def make_spiral(n=200, k=3, noise=0.2, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X, y = [], []
    for c in range(k):
        r = np.linspace(0.05, 1, n); t = np.linspace(c * 4, (c + 1) * 4, n) + rng.normal(0, noise, n)
        X.append(np.c_[r * np.sin(t), r * np.cos(t)]); y += [c] * n
    return torch.tensor(np.vstack(X), dtype=torch.float32), torch.tensor(y)

def train(make_opt, epochs=60, bs=64, seed=0):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    X, y = make_spiral()
    model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 3))
    for m in model:
        if isinstance(m, nn.Linear):
            nn.init.kaiming_normal_(m.weight, nonlinearity="relu"); nn.init.zeros_(m.bias)
    opt = make_opt(model.parameters())
    curve = []
    for ep in range(epochs):
        perm, total = torch.randperm(len(X)), 0.0
        for i in range(0, len(X), bs):
            idx = perm[i:i + bs]
            opt.zero_grad()
            loss = nn.functional.cross_entropy(model(X[idx]), y[idx])
            loss.backward()
            opt.step()
            total += loss.item() * len(idx)
        curve.append(total / len(X))
    return curve

for name, mk in [("SGD", lambda p: torch.optim.SGD(p, lr=0.05)),
                 ("SGD+momentum", lambda p: torch.optim.SGD(p, lr=0.05, momentum=0.9)),
                 ("Nesterov", lambda p: torch.optim.SGD(p, lr=0.05, momentum=0.9, nesterov=True)),
                 ("RMSprop", lambda p: torch.optim.RMSprop(p, lr=1e-3)),
                 ("Adam", lambda p: torch.optim.Adam(p, lr=3e-3)),
                 ("AdamW", lambda p: torch.optim.AdamW(p, lr=3e-3, weight_decay=0.01))]:
    c = train(mk)
    print(f"{name:13s} loss at epochs 1/10/60: {c[0]:.3f} {c[9]:.3f} {c[59]:.3f}")

Common mistakes and debugging tips

Symptom Likely cause Fix
Loss is nan after a few steps Learning rate too high; exploding gradient; log(0); fp16 overflow Lower lr by 3-10x, add warmup and clipping, use bf16 or a loss scaler
Loss flat at ln⁡K\ln KlnK from the start Learning rate too small, init too small, dead ReLUs, labels not matching inputs Run an lr sweep; check init stats; overfit a 32-example batch
Loss decreases then suddenly spikes LR too high late in a long run, Adam ε\varepsilonε/β2\beta_2β2​ issues, a bad batch Clip gradients; lower peak lr; use β2=0.95\beta_2=0.95β2​=0.95 for large models; use cosine decay
Adam converges but generalizes worse than SGD Weak or coupled weight decay Use AdamW, tune λ\lambdaλ, no decay on biases and norm parameters
Weight decay "does nothing" in Adam Using Adam(weight_decay=...) (L2 inside the gradient) Switch to AdamW
Training is fine, eval accuracy is erratic BatchNorm in train mode at eval, or tiny batch statistics model.eval(); use GroupNorm/LayerNorm for tiny batches
Moved to bigger batch, accuracy dropped LR not rescaled, no warmup Scale lr (linear for SGD, sqrt for Adam), warm up, retune the schedule
Scheduler seems to have no effect scheduler.step() not called, called per epoch instead of per step, or called before optimizer.step() Call optimizer.step() then scheduler.step(); check optimizer.param_groups[0]["lr"]
Gradients of first layers are tiny, last layers huge Vanishing gradients: saturating activation, bad init, no normalization He/Glorot init, ReLU/GELU, add norm layers and residual connections
Clipping fires every step lr far too high Lower lr; clipping is a safety net only

Three habits catch most optimization bugs: (1) log training loss, gradient norm, the learning rate and update-to-weight ratio ∥ηg∥/∥θ∥\norm{\eta g}/\norm{\theta}∥ηg∥/∥θ∥ (healthy is around 10−310^{-3}10−3); (2) overfit one small batch to prove the pipeline can learn; (3) change one thing at a time and always compare optimizers at their own tuned learning rates.

Exercises

Exercise 1: Stability of gradient descent on a quadratic

For f(θ)=12λθ2f(\theta)=\tfrac12\lambda\theta^2f(θ)=21​λθ2 derive the condition on η\etaη for gradient descent to converge, and the iterates after ttt steps. What is the best learning rate for f(θ)=12(100θ12+θ22)f(\boldsymbol\theta)=\tfrac12(100\theta_1^2+\theta_2^2)f(θ)=21​(100θ12​+θ22​) and how many steps to shrink the error by 10−310^{-3}10−3?

Solution

θt+1=θt−ηλθt=(1−ηλ)θt\theta_{t+1}=\theta_t-\eta\lambda\theta_t=(1-\eta\lambda)\theta_tθt+1​=θt​−ηλθt​=(1−ηλ)θt​, so θt=(1−ηλ)tθ0\theta_t=(1-\eta\lambda)^t\theta_0θt​=(1−ηλ)tθ0​, convergent iff ∣1−ηλ∣<1|1-\eta\lambda|<1∣1−ηλ∣<1, i.e. 0<η<2/λ0<\eta<2/\lambda0<η<2/λ. For the two-dimensional case the best rate is η⋆=2/(100+1)≈0.0198\eta^\star=2/(100+1)\approx0.0198η⋆=2/(100+1)≈0.0198 with rate ρ=(100−1)/(100+1)≈0.980\rho=(100-1)/(100+1)\approx0.980ρ=(100−1)/(100+1)≈0.980; ρt=10−3\rho^t=10^{-3}ρt=10−3 gives t=ln⁡(10−3)/ln⁡(0.980)≈340t=\ln(10^{-3})/\ln(0.980)\approx340t=ln(10−3)/ln(0.980)≈340 steps. With momentum at the optimal setting the rate becomes (100−1)/(100+1)=9/11≈0.82(\sqrt{100}-1)/(\sqrt{100}+1)=9/11\approx0.82(100​−1)/(100​+1)=9/11≈0.82, so about 35 steps.

Exercise 2: Variance of the mini-batch gradient

Per-example gradients have mean G\boldsymbol GG and covariance Σ\boldsymbol\SigmaΣ. Show that for BBB independent samples, E∥gB−G∥2=tr⁡(Σ)/B\E\norm{\boldsymbol g_B-\boldsymbol G}^2=\tr(\boldsymbol\Sigma)/BE∥gB​−G∥2=tr(Σ)/B. If tr⁡Σ=50\tr\boldsymbol\Sigma=50trΣ=50 and ∥G∥2=0.5\norm{\boldsymbol G}^2=0.5∥G∥2=0.5, what is the noise scale and what does it suggest for batch size?

Solution

gB−G=1B∑i(ξi)\boldsymbol g_B-\boldsymbol G=\frac1B\sum_i(\boldsymbol\xi_i)gB​−G=B1​∑i​(ξi​) with independent zero-mean ξi\boldsymbol\xi_iξi​, so the expected squared norm is 1B2∑iE∥ξi∥2=tr⁡(Σ)/B\frac1{B^2}\sum_i\E\norm{\boldsymbol\xi_i}^2=\tr(\boldsymbol\Sigma)/BB21​∑i​E∥ξi​∥2=tr(Σ)/B. Noise scale =tr⁡Σ/∥G∥2=100=\tr\boldsymbol\Sigma/\norm{\boldsymbol G}^2=100=trΣ/∥G∥2=100. Below about B=100B=100B=100 the gradient is noise-dominated and larger batches are nearly free in terms of steps; far above 100 extra examples buy little per step.

Exercise 3: Bias correction by hand

Run two Adam steps (β1=0.9\beta_1=0.9β1​=0.9, β2=0.999\beta_2=0.999β2​=0.999, ε=0\varepsilon=0ε=0, η=0.1\eta=0.1η=0.1) on a scalar with constant gradient g=2g=2g=2. Compute m,v,m^,v^m,v,\hat m,\hat vm,v,m^,v^ and the updates, with and without bias correction.

Solution

Step 1: m1=0.2m_1=0.2m1​=0.2, v1=0.004v_1=0.004v1​=0.004; m^1=0.2/0.1=2\hat m_1=0.2/0.1=2m^1​=0.2/0.1=2, v^1=0.004/0.001=4\hat v_1=0.004/0.001=4v^1​=0.004/0.001=4, update =0.1⋅2/2=0.1=0.1\cdot2/2=0.1=0.1⋅2/2=0.1. Without correction the update would be 0.1⋅0.2/0.004=0.3160.1\cdot0.2/\sqrt{0.004}=0.3160.1⋅0.2/0.004​=0.316 (too big, since vvv is biased more than mmm). Step 2: m2=0.38m_2=0.38m2​=0.38, v2=0.007996v_2=0.007996v2​=0.007996; m^2=0.38/0.19=2\hat m_2=0.38/0.19=2m^2​=0.38/0.19=2, v^2=0.007996/0.001999=4\hat v_2=0.007996/0.001999=4v^2​=0.007996/0.001999=4, update 0.10.10.1 again. With constant gradients the corrected update is always η sign(g)\eta\,\mathrm{sign}(g)ηsign(g).

Exercise 4: Derive the He variance backward

Repeat the He derivation for the backward pass of a ReLU layer and show the variance condition is σw2=2/nout\sigma_w^2=2/n_{\rm out}σw2​=2/nout​. Why does it not matter much which one you pick?

Solution

aˉi=∑j=1noutwijzˉj\bar a_i=\sum_{j=1}^{n_{\rm out}}w_{ij}\bar z_jaˉi​=∑j=1nout​​wij​zˉj​ and zˉj=aˉj′ 1[zj>0]\bar z_j=\bar a'_j\,\mathbb 1[z_j>0]zˉj​=aˉj′​1[zj​>0], so E[zˉj2]=12E[aˉj′2]\E[\bar z_j^2]=\tfrac12\E[\bar a_j'^2]E[zˉj2​]=21​E[aˉj′2​]. Then Var⁡(aˉi)=noutσw2⋅12Var⁡(aˉ′)\Var(\bar a_i)=n_{\rm out}\sigma_w^2\cdot\tfrac12\Var(\bar a')Var(aˉi​)=nout​σw2​⋅21​Var(aˉ′), which is constant iff σw2=2/nout\sigma_w^2=2/n_{\rm out}σw2​=2/nout​. Over a whole network the fan-in and fan-out conditions differ by the ratio nin/noutn_{\rm in}/n_{\rm out}nin​/nout​ at each layer, and these ratios telescope along a chain of layers (the product of nℓ−1/nℓn_{\ell-1}/n_\ellnℓ−1​/nℓ​ is n0/nLn_0/n_Ln0​/nL​), so using either rule changes the overall scale only by a bounded factor, not an exponential one.

Exercise 5: Why weight decay and L2 differ under Adam

For a scalar parameter with g=0g=0g=0 in the data term (so only the penalty acts), compare the Adam-with-L2 update and the AdamW update in steady state with θ=1\theta=1θ=1, λ=0.1\lambda=0.1λ=0.1, η=0.01\eta=0.01η=0.01.

Solution

Adam+L2: the gradient is λθ=0.1\lambda\theta=0.1λθ=0.1, and in steady state m^≈0.1\hat m\approx0.1m^≈0.1, v^≈0.1\sqrt{\hat v}\approx0.1v^​≈0.1, so the update is η⋅1=0.01\eta\cdot1=0.01η⋅1=0.01 in magnitude: the parameter loses 0.01 per step regardless of λ\lambdaλ (the scaling cancels λ\lambdaλ!). If the data gradient were large with v≈10\sqrt v\approx10v​≈10, the same penalty would move by only 0.01⋅0.1/10=10−40.01\cdot0.1/10=10^{-4}0.01⋅0.1/10=10−4: decay is switched off for parameters with big gradients. AdamW: the decay is ηλθ=10−3\eta\lambda\theta=10^{-3}ηλθ=10−3 per step in both cases. This is the difference: AdamW's decay strength is independent of gradient history.

Exercise 6: BatchNorm gradient identities

Using the BatchNorm backward formula, show that ∑nxˉn=0\sum_n\bar x_n=0∑n​xˉn​=0 and ∑nxˉnx^n=0\sum_n\bar x_n\hat x_n=0∑n​xˉn​x^n​=0.

Solution

Let un=x^ˉnu_n=\bar{\hat x}_nun​=x^ˉn​. Then ∑nxˉn∝B∑un−B∑um−(∑nx^n)(∑umx^m)=0\sum_n\bar x_n\propto B\sum u_n-B\sum u_m-(\sum_n\hat x_n)(\sum u_m\hat x_m)=0∑n​xˉn​∝B∑un​−B∑um​−(∑n​x^n​)(∑um​x^m​)=0 because ∑nx^n=0\sum_n\hat x_n=0∑n​x^n​=0. For the second, ∑nx^nxˉn∝B∑unx^n−∑x^n∑um−∑nx^n2∑umx^m\sum_n\hat x_n\bar x_n\propto B\sum u_n\hat x_n-\sum\hat x_n\sum u_m-\sum_n\hat x_n^2\sum u_m\hat x_m∑n​x^n​xˉn​∝B∑un​x^n​−∑x^n​∑um​−∑n​x^n2​∑um​x^m​, and ∑nx^n2=B\sum_n\hat x_n^2=B∑n​x^n2​=B (up to ε\varepsilonε), so the first and third terms cancel and the middle term is 0. So the gradient wrt the layer input is orthogonal to both the constant vector and x^\hat xx^: shifting or scaling the batch cannot change the loss.

Exercise 7: Code: reproduce the linear scaling rule

Using the lab code, train with batch sizes 16, 32, 64, 128 on the spiral with η=0.05⋅B/32\eta=0.05\cdot B/32η=0.05⋅B/32 and count the optimizer steps needed to reach a training loss below 0.3. Do larger batches follow the rule? Where does it break?

Solution

Wrap run so that it records the first step at which the epoch loss drops below 0.3 (modify it to evaluate the full-data loss every few steps). You should see the steps-to-target fall roughly in inverse proportion to BBB for small BBB (compare the chart earlier in the page, which used plain SGD). It breaks when BBB approaches the noise scale or the dataset size: with B=600B=600B=600 (the full data) there is no noise left to average, the gradient is exact, and the step count is limited by curvature (the largest stable η\etaη), not by BBB. Raising η\etaη proportionally past the stable value diverges; warmup or a lower multiplier fixes that.

Exercise 8: What would happen if (challenging)

You train a ReLU network with He init and BatchNorm after every linear layer, but you then multiply every weight matrix by 100 at initialization. What changes in the forward pass, in the gradients, and in the effective learning rate?

Solution

Forward: nothing, because BN removes the scale: BN(c Wa)=BN(Wa)\mathrm{BN}(c\,\mathbf W\boldsymbol a)=\mathrm{BN}(\mathbf W\boldsymbol a)BN(cWa)=BN(Wa) (up to ε\varepsilonε). Gradients: the loss is invariant to the scale ccc of W\mathbf WW, so the gradient is orthogonal to W\mathbf WW and scales as 1/c1/c1/c (the function depends on the direction W/∥W∥\mathbf W/\norm{\mathbf W}W/∥W∥ only; by homogeneity ∇L(cW)=1c∇L(W)\nabla L(c\mathbf W)=\tfrac1c\nabla L(\mathbf W)∇L(cW)=c1​∇L(W)). A gradient step of size η/c\eta/cη/c on a weight of norm c∥W∥c\norm{\mathbf W}c∥W∥ rotates the direction by an angle of order η/c2\eta/c^2η/c2: the effective learning rate on the direction is divided by c2=104c^2=10^4c2=104, and training effectively freezes. Conversely, weight decay shrinks ccc and so raises the effective learning rate. This scale-invariance explains why BN networks tolerate poor init but interact strongly with weight decay.

Exercise 9: Design a schedule (challenging)

You will train a transformer with AdamW for 100,000 steps at a peak rate of 6×10−46\times10^{-4}6×10−4. Specify a schedule and justify warmup length, final rate, weight-decay settings and clipping.

Solution

A reasonable specification: linear warmup over 2,000 steps (about 2 percent), then cosine decay to 6×10−56\times10^{-5}6×10−5 (10 percent of peak) at step 100,000; AdamW with β=(0.9,0.95)\beta=(0.9,0.95)β=(0.9,0.95), ε=10−8\varepsilon=10^{-8}ε=10−8, weight decay 0.1 on weight matrices only (not biases, LayerNorm gains or embeddings by convention), global-norm clipping at 1.0. Justification: warmup protects against early instability when the second-moment estimate and the attention logits are poorly calibrated; β2=0.95\beta_2=0.95β2​=0.95 makes vvv adapt within about 20 steps, which reacts faster to loss spikes; the nonzero final rate avoids over-committing to the last few steps and cosine is parameter-free apart from the horizon. These numbers are conventional starting points used by several open LLM recipes, not guarantees: tune the peak rate first.

Key takeaways

Key takeaways
  • Neural loss surfaces are non-convex but mostly benign: high-dimensional critical points are overwhelmingly saddles, and the real difficulty is ill-conditioning (a large ratio of curvatures) rather than bad local minima. Flatness is suggestive but parameterization-dependent.
  • Mini-batch gradients are unbiased with covariance Σ/B\boldsymbol\Sigma/BΣ/B; batch size trades steps for compute, and the linear scaling rule (with warmup) works until the batch exceeds the gradient noise scale.
  • Momentum accelerates along consistent directions (O(κ)→O(κ)O(\kappa)\to O(\sqrt\kappa)O(κ)→O(κ​) on quadratics); adaptive methods rescale each coordinate; Adam adds bias-corrected first and second moments; AdamW decouples weight decay and is the default for transformers.
  • Use warmup, then cosine (or step) decay; one-cycle and cyclical schedules are useful when training budgets are short.
  • Initialize with σw2=2/nin\sigma_w^2=2/n_{\rm in}σw2​=2/nin​ for ReLU (He) and 2/(nin+nout)2/(n_{\rm in}+n_{\rm out})2/(nin​+nout​) for tanh (Glorot) so that activation and gradient variances stay constant with depth; clip gradients by global norm as a safety net.
  • Normalization (BatchNorm for large-batch CNNs, LayerNorm/RMSNorm for transformers, GroupNorm for small batches) stabilizes scales, smooths the landscape and allows larger learning rates; BatchNorm behaves differently in train and eval.
  • Compare optimizers only at tuned learning rates, change one variable at a time, log gradient norms, and overfit a small batch first.
